title: Can folding paper make the marks of a protractor?
description: A paper circle is cut into a semicircle and folded in half again and again, and the creases are the equally spaced marks of a protractor. Keeko's doubt, that the marks come out ten degrees apart, is broken by counting the equal parts.
teaching_notes: One idea: each half fold halves the last angle, so three folds make eight equal parts of a straight angle. Watch for children who expect round-number marks.

source: Make your own protractor by paper folding. 1. Draw a circle of a convenient radius on a sheet of paper. Cut out the circle. A circle or one full turn is 360°. 2. Fold the circle to get two equal halves and cut it through the crease to get a semicircle. Write '0°' in the bottom right corner of the semicircle. 3. Fold the semi-circular sheet in half to form a quarter circle. 4. Fold the sheet again. 5. Continue with another half fold. 6. Unfold and mark the creases as OB, OC, ..., etc. (2.9 Make your own protractor, pages 37 to 39)
video_script.why: The child sees that three half folds of a paper semicircle make the equally spaced marks of a protractor.
video_script.substitution: The book's paper circle, cut into a semicircle and folded in half again and again.
video_script.anchor: the book's paper circle, cut into a semicircle and folded three times
video_script.wrong_answer: the marks will come out ten degrees apart
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the marks will come out ten degrees apart. Ten degrees apart would need eighteen parts, but three half folds give only eight equal parts, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The creases make marks every twenty two point five degrees from zero to one hundred and eighty

final_answer.spoken: the marks are zero, twenty two point five, forty five, sixty seven point five, ninety, one hundred twelve point five, one hundred thirty five, one hundred fifty seven point five and one hundred eighty degrees

maths_rules: a full turn is 360 degrees; the first cut gives a semicircle, 360 / 2 = 180 degrees
each half fold halves the last angle: 180 / 2 = 90, 90 / 2 = 45, 45 / 2 = 22.5
three half folds give 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 equal parts of the straight angle, each 22.5 degrees
ten degrees apart would need 180 / 10 = 18 parts, but three folds give 8
video_script.design: The paper semicircle stays on the board. Each fold line appears one after another, and the full list of marks is written only in the answer beat.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko says the marks will come out ten degrees apart.
<bookmark mark='need'/>Ten degrees apart would need eighteen equal parts, because one hundred and eighty divided by ten is eighteen.
